metadata.title: What MP3 Throws Away
metadata.note: Audio-concept explainer: lossy compression. Through-line: an MP3 is not a smaller copy, it is an edited one — the encoder models your ear, finds what you cannot hear, and deletes it permanently. Sibling to the stem-separation reel: both are about information that is gone rather than hidden. Seven beats: four purpose-built scenes (B01/B02/B03/B04), one library ClaudeWindow (B05), ClaudeComposerAsk opener (B00), ClaudeTitleOutro (B06). EVERY NUMBER ON SCREEN WAS MEASURED on this machine with ffmpeg + libmp3lame — see MEASUREMENTS.txt; nothing is quoted from memory. NAME PRONUNCIATION: narration_text spells the presenter phonetically as 'Row-Haan VeeJayKooMaar' so Kokoro says it correctly; all ON-SCREEN text keeps the correct spelling 'Rohan Vijaykumar'.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Row-Haan, for Humanitarians AI. An MP3 is not a smaller copy of your song. It's a different song — one where an algorithm decided which parts you wouldn't miss, and then deleted them permanently. By the end of this you'll know exactly what gets thrown away, and when that matters.

props.command: When I save a song as an MP3, what actually gets removed — and when does that removal start to matter?
output: the encoder models your ear, not the signal

beats.narration_text: Here's white noise — every frequency, equal energy. Now encode it at a hundred and twenty-eight kilobits and look again. Everything above sixteen kilohertz is gone. Not quieter — gone. I measured this on my own machine: at seventeen kilohertz the encoded file is thirteen decibels down. That shelf is the first thing every encoder throws away.

Why sixteen kilohertz? Because the encoder is not trying to preserve the signal. It's modelling your ear. When a loud sound and a quiet sound sit close together in frequency, you physically cannot hear the quiet one — the loud one masks it. The encoder finds every masked sound and spends no bits on it. That's the whole trick: it deletes what you were never going to hear.

props.sparkLine: It deletes what you were never going to hear.

beats.narration_text: So the bitrate decides how aggressive that deletion is. At a hundred and twenty-eight kilobits, the file is eleven times smaller than the original — and the cliff sits at sixteen kilohertz. At three-twenty, it's about four and a half times smaller, and the audio survives intact all the way to nineteen. Same song, same encoder. The only difference is how much the algorithm was allowed to discard.

props.footnote: Measured here: 10s of white noise, ffmpeg + libmp3lame. Exact cliff frequency is encoder-dependent; the shape is not.
props.sparkLine: Same song. Different permission to discard.

beats.narration_text: Here's the part that catches people. Every re-encode starts the deletion over. I took a hundred-and-twenty-eight kilobit file and encoded it ten more times. The twelve kilohertz band lost seven decibels. Each pass throws away a little more, and none of it comes back. Editing an MP3 and re-exporting it is not a neutral operation.

So when is lossy fine? Listening, streaming, sharing a rough mix — a well-encoded three-twenty file is genuinely transparent for almost everyone. When is it malpractice? Archiving. Mastering. Anything you'll edit later, or feed to a model. Keep a lossless master, and export lossy at the very end, once. Never work from the thing that has already been thinned.

props.artifactTitle: When lossy is fine, and when it is not
artifactLines: Fine: listening, streaming, sharing a rough mix. 320 is transparent for almost everyone.
Not fine: archives, masters, anything you will edit again, anything a model will train on.
Keep the lossless master. Export lossy at the very end, one time.
Never edit the file that has already been thinned.
props.sparkLine: Never work from the thing that has already been thinned.

beats.narration_text: An MP3 isn't compressed. It's edited — by an algorithm, on your behalf, permanently. I'm Row-Haan VeeJayKooMaar, for Humanitarians AI.
